title: Which point of the cross section is highest and which is lowest?
description: The seven heights of the cross section are compared as numbers: the positive ones above the sea level line and the negative ones below it. The greatest number gives the highest point and the least number gives the lowest point. The slip of calling minus five hundred the least because five hundred looks small is shown.
teaching_notes: One idea: the highest point has the greatest number and the lowest point has the least number, and a point further below zero has a smaller number. Watch for students who pick the smallest number without its sign as the lowest point.

video_script.why: The child compares positive and negative heights to find the highest and the lowest point of the cross section.
video_script.substitution: The book's own cross section with points A to G, the same picture used for reading the heights.
video_script.anchor: the geographical cross section of the book, with a height scale in metres and the sea level line at zero
video_script.payoff_line: The highest point has the greatest height, and the lowest point has the least.

final_answer.value: Highest point A (+1500 m); lowest point D (-1200 m)
final_answer.spoken: the highest point is eigh, at plus fifteen hundred metres, and the lowest point is D, at minus twelve hundred metres

hold_back: Highest point A (+1500 m); lowest point D (-1200 m)
maths_rules: sea level is the zero line, 0 m
heights read from the picture (approximate): A = +1500, B = -500, C = +300, D = -1200, E = +1200, F = -200, G = +100 (metres)
greatest of 1500, 1200, 300, 100 is 1500; every negative number is less than 0
least of -200, -500, -1200 is -1200, because it is furthest below 0
highest point is the one with the greatest height: A; lowest is the one with the least height: D
video_script.design: The same cross section as before, with the seven heights written beside the points. The greatest number is lit at the top, the least number at the bottom.
